newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia Perwaja Steel to make profit by '98.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia Perwaja Steel to make profit by '98.

text.p: A company engaged to rescue Malaysia's Perwaja Steel Sdn Bhd said on Thursday it was confident the ailing national steel plant could make a net profit of 100 million ringgit ($39.7 million) by 1998.

Equal Concept Sdn Bhd, which will run Perwaja until the government finds it a partner, also expects Perwaja's profit to double to 200 million ringgit by 2000, the national Bernama news agency quoted the firm's chief executive Abu Talib Mohamed as saying.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said earlier Thursday that the rescuers of Perwaja need to invest more than a billion ringgit to revive the steel company.
"If we have the confidence, I feel we can revive this plant," Mahathir was quoted saying by Bernama after a visit to the Perwaja plant in eastern Terengganu state.

Perwaja, a 10-year-old pet project of Mahathir, was found earlier this year to have accumulated losses of 2.9 billion ringgit and its previous government-appointed managers were accused of financial mismanagement.
Abu Talib said that since taking over Perwaja in July, Equal Concept has cut costs at the steel plant by 40 percent or 200 million ringgit through the production of "high value" materials.
Efforts were being made to cut another 200 million ringgit in output cost by boosting production and maintaining factory equipment properly, he said.
Abu Talib said Perwaja would be rolling out a new stainless steel grade by early 1998 and saw a strong demand for steel products until 2000.

He said a forged steel grade introduced by Perwaja two months ago for making automotive components had received an encouraging response. Sales for this were estimated at between 20,000-25,000 tonnes annually, he said.
Abu Talib said the equity structure in Perwaja would be left to the government, which was considering various options such as state-guaranteed loans to rebuild the company's finances.

Equal Concept, a joint-venture between Maju Holdings Sdn Bhd and the Lion Group, was then formed to rescue Perwaja. But Lion backed out after it expressed displeasure with the 30 percent stake offered to it, as compared to Maju's 51 percent.

Mahathir said it was imperative that Perwaja be successful as the project reflected the capability of the country's indigenous Malays, or Bumiputra, and his government wanted to recoup the money invested.
"Perwaja was my idea, if it fails, I will be embarrassed," he said.
